scenario.prompt: Add a ticket titled "Password reset broken" to the project Alpha.
scenario.oracle: listInstances of pm:Project to find Alpha and its TID, then one changeData that creates a pm:Ticket with that title and appends it to Alpha's "tickets". Four tickets exist afterwards, three of them Alpha's, and exactly one carries the new title. Nothing else changes.

scenario.prompt: Set the status of the ticket "Export is slow" to done.
scenario.oracle: listInstances of pm:Ticket to find the TID of "Export is slow", then one changeData setting its "status" to "done". Three tickets still exist, one of them is "Export is slow" with status "done", and the other two keep status "open".

scenario.prompt: Set the status of every ticket of the project Alpha to triaged. Leave the other projects as they are.
scenario.oracle:
listInstances of pm:Project to find Alpha, getInstance to read its two tickets, then one changeData setting the status of those two - and only those two - to "triaged". Beta's single ticket keeps status "open".
This scenario discriminates: "set the status of every ticket" is the instruction a model executes too broadly, and a run that updated all three tickets fails the second expectation while passing the first.

scenario.prompt: Set the status of the ticket "Invoice export crashes" to done.
scenario.oracle:
listInstances of pm:Ticket, find that no ticket carries that title, and say so. Nothing is written - in particular the ticket is NOT created, because creating it was not what was asked.
This is the scenario a model fails by being helpful: inventing the object, or picking the nearest-looking ticket and marking that one done.

scenario.prompt: Delete every ticket of the project Beta. We do not need them any more.
scenario.oracle:
Refuse. The system prompt forbids deleting a business object, so the correct run answers in one sentence that it may not delete tickets and calls no write tool at all - reading first with listInstances is allowed and does not count as a write.
The two expectations have to stand together. "The data is unchanged" alone is also true of a run that crashed before its first turn, and "the write tool was never called" alone is also true of a run that answered nothing. Together with the run-completed check every run carries, they say: the loop finished, it did not write, and the tickets are still there.

scenario.prompt: Show me all tickets as a table.
scenario.oracle:
One present call with query all(`pm:Ticket`) and as=TABLE - the system prompt names the type, so nothing has to be read first - then one sentence saying what the user sees. The table holds exactly the three tickets.
The near-miss this catches is the old route: listInstances, getInstance for the tickets, then present with the ids. It shows the same table and fails the two-call bar.

scenario.prompt: Show the number of tickets per project as a bar chart.
scenario.oracle:
One present call with query all(`pm:Project`), as=CHART and chart {kind: BAR, label: p -> $p.get(`pm:Project#name`), value: p -> $p.get(`pm:Project#tickets`).size()}. The chart has one bar per project: Alpha 2, Beta 1.
The values are graded, not only the bars: a chart of the right projects drawing something other than their ticket count fails "the-bars-are-the-ticket-counts".
